videos.title: [Paper Review] Cocoa: Co-Planning and Co-Execution with AI Agents
videos.description:
33Lab Weekly Meeting Paper Review
Presenter: Eunhyuk Koh (Undergraduate Student)
Lab Website: https://33lab.org

----
Paper Information
Title: Cocoa: Co-Planning and Co-Execution with AI Agents
Venue: CHI '26
URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772318.3791673

Abstract
As AI agents take on increasingly long-running tasks involving sophisticated planning and execution, there is a corresponding need for novel interaction designs that enable deeper human-agent collaboration. However, most prior works leverage human interaction to fix “autonomous” workflows that have yet to become fully autonomous or rigidly treat planning and execution as separate stages. Based on a formative study with 9 researchers using AI to support their work, we propose a design that affords greater flexibility in collaboration, so that users can 1) delegate agency to the user or agent via a collaborative plan where individual steps can be assigned; and 2) interleave planning and execution so that plans can adjust after partial execution. We introduce Cocoa, a system that takes design inspiration from computational notebooks to support complex research tasks. A lab study (n = 16) found that Cocoa enabled steerability without sacrificing ease-of-use, and a week-long field deployment (n = 7) showed how researchers collaborated with Cocoa to accomplish real-world tasks.

videos.title: SpatialClaw: Code as the Action Interface for Agentic Spatial Reasoning
videos.description:
SpatialClaw is a training-free framework from NVIDIA (with contributions from KAIST) that uses executable Python code as the action interface for vision-language agents tackling 3D and 4D spatial reasoning. By maintaining a stateful Python kernel preloaded with input frames plus perception and geometry primitives, the agent writes one executable cell per step, inspects intermediate results, and adapts its strategy — outperforming both single-pass code execution and structured tool-call interfaces.

Published on arxiv in June 2026, the paper evaluates SpatialClaw across 20 spatial reasoning benchmarks spanning static and dynamic 3D/4D tasks, reporting 59.9% average accuracy and a gain of 11.2 points over the prior state-of-the-art spatial agent, with consistent improvements across six VLM backbones from two model families.

This video is a deep-dive audio summary of the paper, walking through the motivation, the code-as-action design, the perception and geometry primitives, benchmark results, and ablations. It closes with a Q&A section addressing common questions about the method, its limitations, and how it compares to SpaceTools-Toolshed and pySpatial.

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.25149

 Efficiency at Scale: Pretraining Large Language Models with NVFP4 

This technical report introduces NVFP4, a specialized 4-bit floating-point format designed by NVIDIA to enhance the efficiency of training Large Language Models (LLMs). By utilizing a two-level scaling strategy and smaller micro-blocks, this format significantly improves computational speed and reduces memory usage compared to standard 8-bit alternatives. To maintain accuracy at this reduced precision, the researchers implemented a methodology involving stochastic rounding, Random Hadamard transforms to manage data outliers, and 2D block scaling for consistency. The effectiveness of this approach was validated by successfully pretraining a 12-billion-parameter model on 10 trillion tokens, marking a historic milestone for stable 4-bit precision training. The results demonstrate that NVFP4 can achieve performance benchmarks nearly identical to higher-precision models while offering up to a three-fold boost in mathematical throughput on modern hardware. Ultimately, this work provides a scalable blueprint for reducing the massive energy and compute requirements currently needed to develop frontier artificial intelligence.

videos.title: Open Source vs. Proprietary AI: A Governance Framework
videos.description:
In the fast-evolving landscape of AI, the decision to build on open-source foundations or adopt proprietary, API-based models is more than a technical preference—it is a foundational governance choice. As regulations like the EU AI Act and global standards like ISO 42001 come into force, organizations must balance the demand for transparency and control against the need for reliability, scalability, and ease of use.

In this video, we explore the governance trade-offs between Open Source and Proprietary AI Models. We move past the hype to analyze the risks, compliance responsibilities, and strategic implications of each approach, helping you build a framework that aligns with your organization’s risk appetite and technical maturity.

In this video, you will learn:

The Control vs. Convenience Trade-off: How proprietary vendors substitute operational burden for reduced control, versus the open-source model that grants full transparency at the cost of internal resource demands.

Data Sovereignty and Security: Why regulated industries (Finance, Healthcare, Government) are increasingly favoring self-hosted open-source models to keep sensitive data within their own perimeter.

The Accountability Gap: Navigating the "who is responsible" challenge—from vendor-managed compliance in proprietary systems to the internal governance requirements of managing your own model stack.

Governance Frameworks: How to implement risk-tiered adoption, audit logs, and "responsible" licensing strategies to maintain compliance regardless of the model architecture you choose.
